bionic-reading-converter.formula: For each word W with length L, at strength ratio R (Light 0.3, Medium 0.4, Strong 0.5): bold letters = max(1, round(L x R)) output = W[0..bold] + W[bold..] Whitespace and punctuation are preserved exactly. Example at Medium (R = 0.4), word 'Reading' (L = 7): bold = max(1, round(7 x 0.4)) = max(1, 3) = 3 output = Reading

bionic-reading-converter.workedExample: Input: 'The quick fox' Strength: Medium (40% of each word bolded) Step by step: 1. Word 'The' (3 letters): bold = max(1, round(3 x 0.4)) = max(1, 1) = 1 -> 'The' 2. Word 'quick' (5 letters): bold = max(1, round(5 x 0.4)) = max(1, 2) = 2 -> 'quick' 3. Word 'fox' (3 letters): bold = max(1, round(3 x 0.4)) = max(1, 1) = 1 -> 'fox' Rendered preview shows: T(he) qu(ick) f(ox) with the bracketed starts in bold. Original text is untouched - only bold markup is added.
mistakes: Cranking strength to Strong for a long article — the heavy bolding gets tiring fast; Medium is the sweet spot for most reading.
Assuming it is proven to double your reading speed — the science is thin, so treat it as a skimming aid, not a superpower.
Copying the preview as plain text and expecting the bolding to survive — formatting only carries over in the HTML copy.
Running it on poetry or legal text — the bolding fights the rhythm and precision those texts need.
Expecting it to fix comprehension problems — it guides the eyes, but dense material still needs slow reading.
